newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - U.S. communist party struggles on despite the odds.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. communist party struggles on despite the odds.

text.p: It may be the living definition of a hopeless cause.

The Berlin Wall and the Soviet Union have crumbled and Karl Marx has been knocked off his pedestal. But, from a shabby building in the city that is a shrine to capitalist wealth, a small band of comrades carries on the fight.

Just a few blocks from the glitzy shops of Fifth Avenue and Manhattan's towering skyscrapers, the Communist Party USA is mobilising for the November 5 U.S. presidential elections with the slogan "People before Profits - Tax the Rich!"
"We have our work cut out in the next few weeks," Gus Hall, party leader for more than four decades, told a group of about 100 supporters.
Hall's aim is to get people to vote -- for U.S. President Bill Clinton. Since there is no communist candidate, he says the Democrats are the only choice for now, the "lesser evil".
The main target is Republican challenger Bob Dole and his party, denounced by Hall as "ultra-right neo-Fascists" who want to destroy everything from education to healthcare.
"They want to be free to maim, poison, cripple, kill and pursue the bottom line with total abandon...Under the circumstances, we believe the lesser evil tactic is the only way forward," said Hall.

For the U.S. comrades, it has always been an uphill struggle in a country that prizes wealth and individuality above everything else, and which spent billions of dollars during the Cold War to defeat the Soviet Union.

But the collapse of communism in Eastern Europe and beyond did not deter them here. While parties in Europe reformed and shed much of their ideological baggage after 1989, the U.S. Communist Party has stuck rigidly to the teachings of Marx.
"We had a big struggle and some people left," said party spokeswoman Terry Albano. "But we retained the centrality of the class struggle."

The party does not give membership figures, saying it fears persecution from U.S. authorities. Some estimates put total membership at between 15,000 and 20,000, although independent observers say it is a fraction of the figure.

But the party says greater insecurity, less welfare and huge job cuts in corporate America have swelled the ranks in its local offices across the United States, with African Americans and Hispanics leading the way.
"In the last few years, we have experienced definite growth, people joining off the streets," said Albano.

Despite the claim, most people at the recent election meeting seemed to be white and either middle-aged or elderly, remnants of a past when the party had more members and when organised labour had real power in the United States.

Hall, a former steelworker, is 86 and has led the party since 1959, running several times in U.S. presidential elections and watching the rise and fall of one of the 20th century's defining political movements.
The last time he ran, in 1984, he won just 36,000 votes.
The party headquarters, a nondescript building in one of Manhattan's less prosperous areas, is also showing its age.

A lurching and creaking elevator takes you to the gloomy top-floor boardroom, where black and white pictures of previous party leaders line the walls -- including John Reid, the communist who went to Russia and gave a vivid eyewitness account of the 1917 revolution.

"Fraternal gifts" from parties around the world, many of them no longer in existence, are displayed on dusty shelves; busts of Lenin, Soviet medals, a folded flag from East Germany, a painted plate depicting workers from Bulgaria.
The party's chief propaganda organ, the People's Weekly World, is produced from a shabby newsroom in the building with ageing equipment, a skeleton staff and paltry funds.
"These premises protected against theft by a condition known as extreme poverty," reads a sign on the wall.
"We used to have a correspondent in Moscow," said Albano. "But he died recently. He was in his 80s."

The party's heyday was a long time ago, in the depressed economic times of the 1920s and 1930s. Established at a congress in Chicago in 1919, it attracted workers in heavy industry, fired by the ideals of the new Soviet Union.
By the outbreak of World War Two in 1939, membership stood at a peak of around 75,000.

But the Cold War turned the mood sharply against communism. Republican Senator Joseph McCarthy led the crackdown in the 1950s and many communists -- including Gus Hall -- were jailed. The party was also riven by factional splits and, as heavy industry declined, membership fell.
The party programme is predictable: heavy taxation, cuts in military spending, nationalisation of industry and the banking sector, health care and education for all.
It may be Marxism, but it is also America.

Coffee mugs with the Soviet-style party symbol of hammer and sickle are on sale. You can buy the T-shirt or a video called "History's Challenge". There is even a toll-free number to call if you want to join and a party page on the Internet.
Militant atheism may be part of communism elsewhere in the world, but not here.
"We have a number of members who are believers," said Albano. "Our fight's with capitalism, not with God."
Hall, dressed in a dark suit and red tie, dispenses wit and party wisdom to his enthusiastic followers in a rasping and sometimes halting voice.

He takes questions on world affairs, denouncing Israel's "Zionist imperialist" policies, warning China against ditching communist principles and castigating former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev for destroying the communist world.
"Gorbachev was good but he went haywire," he says. "He literally sold out in the end," he says.
